questions.q: What is a geographic role in Tableau?
options: A tag on a field telling Tableau it represents a real-world location, which enables automatic geocoding against Tableau's built-in database
A user permission level in Tableau Server
A setting that controls which color palette a map uses
A type of calculated field used only in dashboards
questions.explain: A geographic role marks a field as a location, letting Tableau automatically generate Latitude/Longitude values by matching it against its built-in geocoding database.

questions.q: How do you manually assign a geographic role to a field Tableau didn't recognize automatically?
options: Right-click the field in the Data pane, select Geographic Role, and pick the matching role
Rename the field to 'Location' and Tableau assigns it automatically
Geographic roles can only be assigned during the initial data connection
Drag the field onto the Filters shelf
questions.explain: The right-click context menu on any field includes a Geographic Role submenu listing options like Country/Region, State/Province, City, and more.

questions.q: What happens automatically when you drag a field with a geographic role onto the canvas?
options: Tableau populates Longitude on Columns and Latitude on Rows and switches the view to a map
Tableau opens the Edit Relationship dialog
Nothing happens until you also add a measure
Tableau converts the field into a calculated field
questions.explain: Dragging (or double-clicking) a geographic field auto-populates the generated Longitude/Latitude fields onto Columns/Rows and switches to a map view.

questions.q: Where do the 'generated' Latitude and Longitude fields in the Data pane come from?
options: Tableau's own internal geocoding database, matched against the text values in your geographic field
They must be manually typed in by the user for every row
They're imported directly from your source database as regular columns
They come from a separate spatial file you must always connect first
questions.explain: Generated Latitude/Longitude fields are Tableau's own geocoding lookup — not data you provided — matching values like 'Texas' against its internal coordinate database.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why might a generated Latitude/Longitude value come back empty for some rows?
options: A value in your data (a typo or unrecognized abbreviation) doesn't match anything in Tableau's internal geocoding database
Empty Latitude/Longitude values are a random, unavoidable bug with no known cause
It only happens with live connections, never with extracts
It means the field's geographic role must be set to None
questions.explain: When a value doesn't match Tableau's geocoding database, its generated coordinates come back empty and the point can't be plotted — exactly the problem Lesson 56 addresses.
